title: Why Laser Beams Are the Hottest New Tech in Defense
description:
Our guest today is Colonel Sanders. More precisely, we speak with Wayne Sanders, a retired US army colonel who is currently senior defense research analyst for Bloomberg Intelligence. During his military career, Sanders specialized in cybersecurity and weapon systems research and his work for BI has recently focused on directed energy weapon systems — better known as lasers. Just a few decades ago, programs like Star Wars, the Reagan-era missile defense system, seemed like a pipedream; today lasers can shoot down missiles and much more. Sanders tells us about the physics problems researchers had to solve to make laser weapons a reality, why we still don't have laser guns, what makes a weapons system "exquisite," the economic costs that factor into battlefield decisions, and the unique supply chain constraints that affect laser development.

Weary US Sailors Lay Bare War’s Strain During Thailand Shore Leave
German Navy Tests Ballistic Missile for the First Time at Sea

speaker: Wayne Sanders — Senior Defense Research Analyst, Bloomberg Intelligence
one_line_summary: Directed‑energy weapons are moving from laboratory concepts to field‑ready systems, driven by advances in power density and the need to counter low‑cost drone swarms and ballistic threats.
summary:
Wayne Sanders explains that laser and high‑powered microwave (HPM) systems fall under directed‑energy weapons, a subset of electronic warfare. He contrasts a laser as a precision “sniper rifle” that concentrates energy on a single target, with an HPM as an “electronic shotgun” that can disable multiple drones or electronics simultaneously. Sanders notes that the U.S. and Israel are advancing deployment programs—Israel’s Iron Beam (also called Laser Dome) and the U.S. Tactical High Energy Laser (FEL) and DARPA’s MIRACLE—while the U.S. ballistic missile supply is dwindling, making energy weapons attractive for cost‑effective defense. He highlights the historical evolution from 1960s chemical lasers to modern solid‑state lasers, noting that the 2006 program termination was due to size and power constraints. The key technical hurdle remains power: lasers require large, high‑power diodes and can be ship‑ or truck‑mounted only if they can draw from shore power or large batteries, whereas HPM can generate peak powers up to 100 megawatts but still faces deployment challenges.

Key themes include the trade‑off between size, weight, and power (SWaP), the shift from chemical to solid‑state lasers, and the strategic imperative to counter inexpensive aerial threats with high‑energy weapons.

The U.S.'s ballistic missile supply has been dwindling
High powered microwave weapons can generate peak powers up to like 100 megawatts
Laser kilowatt ratings are misleading compared to HPM megawatt ratings

framework_insights: Directed energy is a form of electronic warfare that uses harnessed energy to degrade or destroy targets
A laser is a precision weapon (sniper rifle) while an HPM is a broader‑area weapon (shotgun)
Power density and SWaP tradeoffs dictate whether a system can be deployed on a truck, ship, or fixed base
Historical progression from chemical lasers to solid‑state lasers shows that technological maturity is driven by power availability
The strategic value of directed energy increases when conventional munitions become cost‑prohibitive for low‑value targets
market_relevance: Investors in defense contractors and semiconductor suppliers should watch for shifts in R&D spending toward solid‑state laser components and power electronics, as these firms could benefit from the growing demand for deployable directed‑energy systems.

title: Why Gold Is Expected to Rise to Record Highs
description:
Gold set a record high in January, but uncertainty about US interest rates and disruption from the Iran war have led to an “elongated pause” in the rally, according to Tony Kim, global head of Metals Trading in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. Ultimately, Kim expects strong central bank demand for the yellow metal to help drive gold to new highs, he says on The Markets podcast. Kim also discusses whether fiscal sustainability concerns could spur a rotation into gold, how reduced investment demand from Asia is impacting gold markets, and why silver has been volatile in 2026.

title: From CEO to Startups: Masters in Business with Former Vanguard CEO Bill McNabb
description:
Barry speaks with William "Bill" McNabb. He's former chairman and CEO of Vanguard and now sits on the board at UnitedHealth, IBM, Axiom, and Altruist. They discuss his 30+ years at Vanguard and his career after leaving the company, working in the board room and with startups in fintech and more.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Bill McNabb — former CEO and Chairman, Vanguard Group
one_line_summary: Vanguard’s long‑term success hinged on low‑cost indexing, a deep belief in investor longevity, and a culture of collective teamwork and leading by example.
summary: Bill McNabb recounts his path from a Dartmouth Latin teacher and Haverford School coach to CEO of Vanguard, emphasizing luck, mentorship, and the “we versus I” mindset that shaped Vanguard’s culture. He highlights Vanguard’s early days with $15 billion under management, the rise of money‑market funds with yields in the 17‑18% range, and the firm’s shift to low‑cost indexing after research showed index funds beat 90% of active equities over any rolling 10‑year period. During the 2008 crisis, McNabb describes a strategy of no layoffs, doubling down on service, and educating clients to maintain investor confidence. Post‑crisis, Vanguard expanded its advisor channel, launched target‑date funds, and leveraged behavioral finance research to automate 401(k) enrollment and escalation, positioning these products as default options.

Low‑cost indexing and long‑term investor focus

Money‑market fund yields were "17%, 18% at different times"

market_relevance: Vanguard’s emphasis on low‑cost, long‑term investing and its proven ability to navigate crises offer a benchmark for asset managers today, while its behavioral‑finance‑driven 401(k) strategies illustrate how automation can improve retirement outcomes in a volatile market.

title: What's Behind the Big Surge in US Government Bond Yields
description:
Global bond yields are at their highest level since 2008, with the 30-year US Treasury touching 5% just before Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a surprise increase of his department's bond buyback program and Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh made his hawkish speech at Jackson Hole. So what's driving yields higher? And what options do policymakers have to bring them down? In this episode we speak with Stanford Professor Darrell Duffie, who's been researching bonds for years, including presenting a paper at Jackson Hole in 2023 about how to fix the US Treasury market. A lot has changed since then, and at this year's Jackson Hole symposium, we caught up with Duffie to talk about everything going on in the bond market, as well as the challenge of shrinking the Fed's balance sheet.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Daryl Duffy — Professor of Finance, Stanford University
one_line_summary: US bond yields are climbing because the Treasury’s massive debt supply is outpacing demand from domestic discretionary investors, and Treasury buybacks and Fed actions are not enough to curb the pressure.
summary: The discussion centers on the sharp rise in long‑term US Treasury yields, with the 30‑year now above 5%.  Daryl Duffy explains that the Treasury’s debt has grown from about $18 trillion a decade ago to $31 trillion today, creating a supply shock that domestic investors—mutual funds, hedge funds, banks, insurance companies, pension funds—must absorb.  Foreign central banks have largely stopped buying, leaving the burden on domestic discretionary investors who demand higher yields for the added duration.  Treasury buyback programs, such as the recent expansion announced by Scott Besson, are intended to signal that yields are too high, but the market reaction was short‑lived because the Treasury’s power to set yields is limited.  The Fed is avoiding fiscal dominance and will not engage in yield‑curve control, leaving the Treasury to manage its debt maturity profile, which remains around six years on average.

market_relevance: Investors should monitor the 30‑year yield trend, Treasury debt growth, and the effectiveness of buyback signals, as these factors directly influence borrowing costs and portfolio allocation decisions.

title: Columbia Threadneedle Scans AI Debt Rush for Alpha Opportunity
description:
Columbia Threadneedle is looking to outperform by buying into the flood of debt from companies building artificial intelligence infrastructure. “It’s really the best place to try to find some volatility and some alpha opportunities here, as long as you can remain nimble,” Tom Murphy, the $715 billion manager’s head of investment-grade credit, tells Bloomberg News’ James Crombie and Bloomberg Intelligence’s David Havens in the latest Credit Edge podcast. “If we start to see all of this investment turn into cash flow, it could really be tremendous,” he says. They also discuss fundamental and technical credit market indicators, the September issuance rush and relative value in financial sector bonds.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Tom Murphy — Head of Investment Grade Credit, Columbia Threadneedle Investments
one_line_summary: AI‑driven debt issuance is flooding the market, compressing spreads and forcing credit managers to stay nimble and focus on fundamentals to capture value.
summary:
Columbia Threadneedle notes that investment‑grade credit is under pressure from a surge in AI infrastructure debt, with issuances of $200‑$250 billion from hyperscalers year‑to‑date and $50 billion in IG data‑center deals. Yields are attractive—Bloomberg Corporate Index at 5.4%, long‑duration credit at 6%—but spreads are thin, with the Bloomberg Corporate Index spread at 15% of yield, a 25‑year low. The firm’s strategy is to maintain a fundamentals‑plus‑technicals framework, stay liquid, and avoid over‑exposure to high‑volatility AI debt while capitalizing on solid balance sheets and over‑funded pension funds. They emphasize the need to monitor spreads as a percentage of yield and to be cautious of construction and leasing risks in new AI debt.

Key data points include record IG issuance in June‑August, AI debt’s rapid pace (seven $25 billion deals this year), and the shift from traditional bank debt cadence to hyperscaler‑driven releases. The discussion highlights the importance of understanding the new risk profile of AI debt and the potential for mispricing as the market adjusts.

The conversation underscores that while yields remain enticing, the compressed spreads and rapid issuance pace demand a disciplined, fundamentals‑driven approach to avoid being caught in the “sword of Damocles” of AI debt volatility.

title: Can AI Earn It Back? The $2 Trillion Test and Other Forces Reshaping Markets and Portfolios
description:
Between now and 2030, roughly $5 trillion will be spent building the infrastructure for AI. To justify that investment, businesses and individuals will need to spend $2 trillion a year on AI services. Whether AI can earn back what's being spent on it is a defining question of this investment cycle, with impacts to be felt across debt and equity markets.

Rob Bittencourt, who leads Apollo Thematic Investing, has spent his career tracking exactly these kinds of non-linear shifts.

In this conversation, Rob breaks down the state of AI adoption and what enterprise ROI pressure means for the cycle and investor portfolios. He also discusses two other themes his team is tracking: US reindustrialization and why private capital may be better positioned than public markets to finance it, and the forces that are beginning to reshape finance itself.

For more analysis from Apollo Thematic Investing, check out these links:

The Growing Compute Shortage: https://www.apollo.com/wealth/insights-news/insights/2026/06/growing-compute-shortage

The Balance Sheet Behind the AI Revolution: https://www.apollo.com/wealth/insights-news/insights/2026/03/balance-sheet-behind-the-ai-revolution
speaker: Rob Bittencourt — leads Apollo Thematic Investing
one_line_summary: AI’s rapid adoption is driving a $5 trillion infrastructure spend, but investors must navigate concentration risk and mixed ROI signals across hyperscalers and AI‑canary firms.
summary:
Rob Bittencourt explains that the AI boom, sparked by ChatGPT’s 2022 launch, has accelerated into a multi‑phase cycle: initial hype, compute‑intensive reasoning models, and the recent agentic AI explosion. NVIDIA’s Q2 2023 revenue grew 100% YoY, highlighting the financial impact of AI. The industry is projected to spend roughly $5–6 trillion on AI infrastructure by 2030, with $2 trillion per year on AI‑related services—surpassing the combined size of online advertising ($750–800 bn) and enterprise software (>1 tr). Financing is shifting from free cash flow to investment‑grade bonds, with hyperscalers issuing over $100 bn net last year and $200 bn this year. Meanwhile, a cohort of “AI canaries”—about 200 software and business‑service firms—shows mixed signals: 10 have consensus EBITDA declines, yet valuation multiples are already contracting. Investors face heightened concentration risk as AI exposure permeates equity, high‑yield, and leveraged‑loan markets, especially within the major indices.

Key themes include the accelerating AI cycle, the financing shift toward debt and equity for hyperscalers, and the use of AI canaries as early disruption indicators.

title: At The Money Fan Favorite: Looking Past Market Cap Weighted Indexes
description:
On this special, fan favorite episode, Barry speaks with Rob Arnott, founder of Research Affiliates (RAFI). They discuss how cap weighted indexes have come to dominate ETFs, and why investors should consider a strategy based on fundamental weightings, such as profits or revenue growth.

Each week, “At the Money” discusses an important topic in money management. From portfolio construction to taxes and cutting down on fees, join Barry Ritholtz to learn the best ways to put your money to work.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Rob Arnott — founder of Research Affiliates
one_line_summary: Cap‑weighted indexes drag performance through front‑running and flip‑flop costs; a fundamental, rebalancing index can beat value by ~2%/yr compounded and reduce concentration risk.
summary: Rob Arnott argues that market‑cap weighting concentrates risk in the Magnificent Seven and incurs hidden costs from front‑running and flip‑flop trades. He cites a 15‑basis‑point annual drag from index additions and deletions, and 300‑500 bps per trade when indexers buy at close prices. Flip‑flops cost investors 7,000 bps on deletions and 3,500 bps on pre‑deletion underperformance, while re‑additions can yield 180% outperformance. Arnott proposes a fundamental economic weighting that averages sales, profits, net worth, and dividends, producing a value tilt that has outperformed cap‑weighted value indexes by 2–2.5% per year compounded, with 2.5% tracking error and a 50% wealth advantage after 20 years. He notes that equal weighting shares similar performance but with higher volatility.

300 to 500 basis points per trade due to crowded index trading

Flip‑flop cost model: front‑running and deletion timing create systematic drag
Fundamental weighting: average of sales, profits, net worth, dividends to mirror economy
Rebalancing alpha: trim over‑priced stocks, top under‑priced ones based on fundamentals

market_relevance: Investors facing concentration risk in mega‑cap dominated markets can use a fundamental, rebalancing index to capture value upside while avoiding the hidden costs of cap‑weighted indexing.

title: Cheap North Asian Currencies Reach Turning Point
description:
North Asian currencies – including the Japanese yen, South Korean won, Taiwan dollar and Chinese yuan – are trading at some of their deepest discounts on record, dropping up to 56% below purchasing power parity. These depressed valuations persist despite strong macro fundamentals, backed by massive foreign exchange reserves and their status as top global creditors. However, this valuation gap is beginning to snap back as booming domestic economies, rising retail sales, and increasing inflation prompt central banks in the region to hike interest rates.

What will this shifting macroeconomic environment mean for regional FX and equities? Sean Darby, equity strategist at Mizuho Securities, joins host John Lee on the Asia Centric podcast. Darby unpacks his "Burger Heaven" thesis on undervalued currencies and explains why steepening yield curves are setting up long-ignored bank stocks to outperform.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Sean Darby — equity strategist, Mizuho Securities
one_line_summary: North‑Asian currencies are snapping back from deep discounts as rising rates and trade surpluses lift bank earnings and shift the AI‑bank trade‑off.
summary: Sean Darby explains that the Japanese yen, Korean won, Taiwan dollar and Chinese yuan have been trading 40‑56% below PPP, yet are backed by massive foreign‑exchange reserves and large trade surpluses.  The Bank of Korea’s 25‑basis‑point hike and the expectation of further moves in Korea, Japan and Taiwan are beginning to lift domestic rates, making local assets more attractive and tightening U.S. funding costs.  Retail‑sales growth of 8.4% in Korea and 7.7% in Taiwan, ship‑building orders up 60% and nominal GDP up to 16% YoY illustrate a strong export‑driven boom that is feeding bank profitability (ROE rising from ~5% to >10%).  Meanwhile, China’s CNY is gaining traction through gold backing and offshore settlement reforms, signalling a nascent de‑dollarisation push.  The combination of currency appreciation, higher rates and robust trade fundamentals is creating a tailwind for banks while potentially headwinds for dollar‑priced tech exports.

title: Adam Posen Thinks Things Could Get Very 'Messy' for the Fed
description:
Kevin Warsh gave a hawkish speech at this year's annual Kansas City Fed Symposium in Jackson Hole, but that doesn't mean the challenges are over. Will the Fed actually pull the trigger on rate hikes? What happens if the central bank doesn't act quickly enough to curb inflation? And how exactly will the new chair want to leave his mark on the Fed? In this episode, we speak with Adam Posen, president of the Peterson Institute for International Economics, who gives us his take on the direction of monetary policy and he grades Warsh's speech. We also discuss why high inflation in the US is different than the inflation seen in other countries, how the Treasury's wading into the bond market affects Fed independence, which of the Fed task forces might be the most impactful, the "messy jobs" theory of AI, and what Warsh really means when he says he wants the FOMC to have a “good family fight.”

Get tickets to see Odd Lots live in LA!

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Adam Posen — President, Peterson Institute
one_line_summary: Adam Posen warns that Fed Chair Warsh’s heavy discretion and lack of clear forward guidance could lead to a messy inflation trajectory.
summary:
Adam Posen critiques Fed Chair Warsh’s recent speech, noting its B‑minus rating and the confusion it caused among observers. He highlights Warsh’s emphasis on a 2% core PCE target and his view that wage inflation is not a reliable predictor of overall inflation, while also stressing the importance of financial conditions. Posen expresses concern that Warsh’s preference for last‑minute discretion, rather than a rule‑based approach, risks undermining the Fed’s credibility and could exacerbate inflation if rates are not raised decisively. He contrasts this with the more consensus‑driven cultures of the ECB and BoE, and warns that fiscal dominance—particularly the U.S. fiscal laxity—may pressure the Fed to act more aggressively.

Key points include Warsh’s mixed messaging on inflation speed and direction, the potential for fiscal policy to influence monetary stance, and the historical tension between discretion and accountability in Fed governance.

The discussion underscores the delicate balance the Fed must maintain between flexibility and transparency to preserve its credibility in a high‑inflation environment.

title: The Outlook for Data Center Power Demand as AI Token Use Grows
description:
Global data center power demand could rise 170% by 2030 from 2025 levels according to Goldman Sachs Research’s Brian Singer and Carly Davenport. They joined hosts Allison Nathan and George Lee on the Goldman Sachs Exchanges podcast to  discuss how data centers will source that power, the key bottlenecks, and the impact of growing pushback from some local communities. 

Key takeaways: 

The rise in power demand from AI more broadly is forecast to be the equivalent of adding another Japan to the world’s power consumption by 2030 compared to the start of 2024. 

Goldman Sachs Research sees seven key binding constraints for data center power today including price, policy, and people. Delays for connecting data centers to regional US power grids are as long as seven years. 

The Mid-Atlantic region should remain the largest US data center power market until at least 2030, but the Midwest is set to overtake Texas for second place.

title: Chris Voss on ‘No’-Oriented Questions
description:
Former FBI lead international kidnapping negotiator Chris Voss explains why the best negotiators get out of the “yes” business. Yes-oriented questions make people feel cornered; a well-placed “no”-oriented question gives them the freedom to surface their real objections.

title: Sarah Guo - Funding the Frontier - [Invest Like the Best, EP.489]
description:

Sarah has become one of the most sought-after early-stage investors in AI, often the first check into the companies defining the frontier. 

In this conversation, we go inside that frontier: what the small group of people actually building AI believe right now, why some of the field's best researchers are wrestling with their own sense of purpose, and how close we are to robots in the home and a genuine acceleration in scientific discovery.

title: Richmond Fed’s Tom Barkin on the Surprisingly Resilient Real Economy
description:
The implications of Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech are pretty clear: Traders expect a rate hike given the hawkish hints littered in his address, largely focused on inflation. There are still a number of open questions and Warsh's lack of forward guidance does not exactly lend clarity to how the Fed will act in the coming months. Today, we recap the speech — in a conversation recorded from the Lodge at Jackson Hole — with Richmond Federal Reserve Bank President Tom Barkin and he explains why his thinking around the Fed's communication policy is changing, and he gets into what is still useful about things like the dot plot. He also tells us what he's hearing at Chamber of Commerce meetings about the impact of AI on local communities, how businesses are using their tariff refund checks, and whether the Fed will have to start paying attention to the economic effects of data center politicization.

one_line_summary: The Richmond Fed’s Tom Barkin argues that the U.S. economy remains resilient because consumers are borrowing from the future and spending, even amid high inflation and supply constraints, and that policy should remain cautious about forward guidance.
summary:
Tom Barkin, speaking at Odd Lots, praised Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s speech for its clarity and alignment with his view that the economy is solid, citing strong GDP and consumer spending, low unemployment, and a stable job market. Barkin highlighted that consumers are finding ways to spend—through borrowing, reduced savings rates, and spending on housing and discretionary items—despite high gas prices and inflation. He noted that AI investment is creating construction constraints, especially in data centers, but is not yet delivering a broad productivity boom. Barkin also discussed the Fed’s approach to forward guidance, expressing support for the SEP but cautioning against the dot plot’s potential to mislead markets.

Key points include the resilience of consumer spending driven by future borrowing, the impact of AI on construction labor and materials, and the Fed’s balanced view on transparency versus the risks of over‑guidance.

The transcript ends with Barkin emphasizing the importance of maintaining a clear but flexible policy stance in the face of ongoing inflationary shocks.

title: Daylian Cain on the Theory of the Pie
description:
In this clip from Ted Seides’ conversation with Yale negotiations professor Daylian Cain, Daylian lays out Barry Nalebuff’s “theory of the pie” — the idea that a deal’s real value is the unique synergy two sides cannot create without each other.

Market power shrinks that pie, but it doesn’t hand the stronger party a bigger slice — which is why even the smaller player can fight for half. Essential framing for any allocator negotiating fees, terms, or a co-investment with a larger counterpart.

title: Austan Goolsbee Is Worried the Economy Is Overheating
description:
Inflation remains high and the 2% target is farther away than it was this time last year. There are signs all over that the economy is overheating — the strange labor market where hiring and firing remains low, while GDP is growing, but mostly due to AI and the data center buildout — and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee is worried about how uncertain central bankers are about what to do to cool the economy. The next shock, he tells us, could be around the corner. In this conversation, recorded at the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium, Goolsbee explains why he is skeptical of metrics like r*, why he is embracing Kevin Warsh's philosophy around reducing forward guidance, the purpose of the new Fed task forces, and the economic indicators that influence his thinking around reaction function.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Austin Goolsbee — President, Chicago Fed
one_line_summary: The Fed’s policy is still too restrictive given persistent inflation and supply shocks, but AI‑driven productivity gains could eventually lift the neutral rate and justify higher long‑term rates.
summary:
Austin Goolsbee argues that the Fed’s current stance is restrictive, citing a real rate of about 1% with 3% rates and 2% inflation as an eventual landing spot. He stresses that inflation remains warm and that supply shocks—tariffs, war‑driven oil price spikes, and AI‑related investment—are driving price pressures. Goolsbee notes that AI may raise the neutral rate by boosting productivity, but the current six months of weak productivity growth temper that optimism. He credits the Fed’s aggressive rate hikes for preventing a runaway inflation spiral, while warning that the market’s long‑term yields rising may reflect expectations of higher rates or continued inflation.

Key themes include the difficulty of measuring the neutral rate (R‑star), the role of supply shocks versus demand in inflation dynamics, the potential productivity impact of AI, and the importance of the Fed’s aggressive policy in anchoring inflation expectations.

The discussion highlights that the Fed’s policy is still restrictive, that AI investment is tightening supply chains and potentially overheating the economy, and that long‑term yields are rising as markets anticipate higher rates or persistent inflation.

title: The Science Behind The Markets: Masters in Business with David Booth
description:
Barry speaks with David Booth, founder and chairman at Dimensional Fund Advisors and author of Stay Calm. They discuss his time at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business where he was the research assistant to American economist and Nobel Laureate Eugene Fama, before leaving to start Dimensional Fund Advisors. They discuss embracing the uncertainty of the markets and the importance of staying the course. David also discusses his philanthropic history and giving back to the places that shaped him.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: David Booth — Founder, Dimensional Funds
one_line_summary: David Booth explains how data‑driven research proved that most professionals cannot beat the market, leading to the rise of index investing and the success of Dimensional’s factor‑based strategies.
summary:
David Booth recounts his academic roots at the University of Chicago, the development of the CRISP database in 1963, and the early evidence that professional managers rarely outperform the market—only 27% beat the index last year and less than half do so in any given year. He describes how this insight spurred the creation of the first index fund at Wells Fargo for Samsonite and the early small‑cap focus that became the foundation of Dimensional. Booth emphasizes the importance of empirical data over anecdotal claims, the role of commission‑based sales in perpetuating active trading, and the shift toward low‑cost, diversified, factor‑based investing.

Key themes include the empirical validation of the Efficient Market Hypothesis, the historical emergence of index funds, the strategic use of small‑cap and beta factors, and the critique of commission‑driven active management.

title: ‘Things Are Going to Get Crazier’: AI Debt Deluge Recalls 2007 Risks
description:
Massive borrowing by artificial intelligence companies — some of it to fund their own customers — risks inflating a technology-sector bubble, according to Seaport Research Partners. “Things are going to get crazier,” Jay Goldberg, the firm’s senior analyst for semiconductors and electronics, tells Bloomberg News’ James Crombie and Bloomberg Intelligence’s Robert Schiffman in the latest Credit Edge podcast. “All this debt is coming on stream, it’s going to amp up things even further — this feels to me like 2007,” Goldberg says. “There are certainly corners of the industry that are prone to blow ups.” They also discuss AI vigilantes, concentration risk and growing anxiety about circular financing.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Jay Goldberg — senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners
one_line_summary: AI debt surge is fueled by circular financing that may become a risk as demand saturates, but the long‑term payoff hinges on continued AI model improvement.
summary:
The discussion centers on the unprecedented scale of debt issuance by hyperscalers to fund AI infrastructure, with NVIDIA and other chip makers providing financing to data‑center developers. Jay Goldberg notes signs of a bubble in the data‑center complex and highlights the circular financing model where chip makers invest in customers who then buy chips, potentially creating a feedback loop. He warns that as AI capacity matures, demand could taper, exposing the backstop commitments and contingent liabilities that are currently off‑balance‑sheet. Despite these risks, Goldberg remains cautiously optimistic, arguing that the pace of AI model improvement could justify the massive CapEx, though the real ROI will only be visible at a GDP scale. The conversation also touches on the lack of compelling consumer use cases and the modest efficiency gains seen in enterprise pilots, suggesting that the current investment may be over‑hyped relative to near‑term monetization.

Key points include the scale of CapEx ($800 billion this year, at least $1 trillion next year), the concentration of funding among seven tech giants, and the potential for circular financing to become a liability when demand slows. The debate reflects a broader tension between bullish expectations of AI’s transformative power and bearish concerns about over‑leveraging and speculative growth.

title: Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid on the First Jackson Hole of the Warsh Era
description:
We are back in Jackson Hole! And this year's Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City symposium on monetary policy might be one of the most interesting editions in years. It marks the first under new Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, and Fed observers all over the world will be closely watching his Friday speech for signs of how he might further distinguish himself, and the institution he is in charge of, from the Jerome Powell era. This meeting at Jackson Hole also comes at a fascinating, and pretty tense, time for monetary policy in the US and abroad: high bond yields, above-target inflation, and AI's still unrealized effect on broader parts of the economy like the job market. As we have in the past, we speak with Jeffrey Schmid, the president and CEO of the Kansas City Fed, about what to expect and he also shares his thoughts on the wave of baby boomer retirements and how it's affecting the labor force, his recent FOMC votes, and he explains why this symposium is so focused on payments.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Jeff Schmidt — Kansas City Fed President
one_line_summary: Jeff Schmidt highlights that instant payments and AI‑driven data center growth are reshaping credit demand, while a 30‑year yield above 5% signals a normalized but still volatile yield curve that could tighten inflation expectations.
summary:
Schmidt discusses the Kansas City Fed’s focus on financial innovation, noting that atomic settlement will make payments instant and require proven liquidity. He links this to the current yield curve, where the 30‑year yield is above 5%, and argues that a growing economy between 2% and 3.5% is keeping the curve fairly normalized. He also stresses the labor‑force shift as baby boomers retire, creating both opportunities and risks, and explains how AI and data‑center expansion are driving commodity demand and influencing credit competition between commercial and public sectors. Finally, he describes the FOMC dissent process as a mechanism to balance inflation and employment mandates and comments on the new “family fight” style of debate under Chairman Warsh.

Key points include the importance of liquidity for instant payments, the role of the 30‑year yield as a policy signal, the impact of AI on credit demand, the labor‑force transition, and the procedural nature of FOMC dissent.

The discussion underscores how technology, labor dynamics, and yield curve movements intersect to shape monetary policy and market expectations.

one_line_summary: Dividend growth investing delivers superior returns by focusing on companies that generate real economic profit, not just market price swings.
summary: David Bonson argues that true investing is about owning a company’s underlying profits, not speculating on price movements. He distinguishes between endogenous returns—growth driven by a firm’s own performance—and exogenous returns—price changes driven by market sentiment. Bonson cites recent market data: the S&P 500 rose nearly threefold over seven years, dipped 5% in 2018, and fell 18% in 2022, while dividend growth outperformed the market by 400–500 basis points in the same period. He stresses that dividend-paying firms can maintain discipline, avoid reckless M&A, and still pursue value‑creating acquisitions. Finally, he warns that the current speculative environment, amplified by options and prediction markets, can distort valuations and that a dividend strategy can help investors benefit from volatility rather than merely endure it.

title: Europe Needs €14 Trillion to Catch US, China
description:
After decades of lagging behind the US and China in economic growth and innovation, Europe faces a stark reality: the era of cheap Russian energy, low-cost Chinese goods and US-backed security is over. Achieving strategic self-sufficiency will cost an estimated €14 trillion through 2035, according to Bloomberg Intelligence, requiring massive capital deployment across defense, energy, technology and agriculture. Traditional industrial mainstays are also under threat, with Chinese EV makers rapidly capturing market share and endangering an auto sector that employs nearly 14 million people.

Rod Turnbull, EMEA research content manager at Bloomberg Intelligence, joins John Lee on the Asia Centric podcast. Turnbull breaks down how Europe can fund this €1.5 trillion annual effort — from unlocking €11 trillion in consumer bank deposits to EU budget shifts. He also highlights key investment opportunities across defense and tech, while weighing whether political friction and national self-interest could derail execution.

Current GDP growth is 1.2% versus the U.S. 2%+, and the GDP gap is about €3 trillion, potentially widening to $7 trillion by 2040 if unaddressed. Funding could come from unlocking €11 trillion of EU citizens’ deposits, pension fund restructuring in Germany (~€500 billion), the Multi‑Annual Financial Framework (MFF) budget shift, and the SAFE program providing €150 billion in low‑cost loans. Defense is seen as the most achievable area, with European primes like Rheinmetall, BAE Systems, Saab, and niche firms such as Theon and Mildef positioned for growth.

title: The Nigerian Industrial Behemoth That Could Reshape the African Economy
description:
Earlier in August, it was reported that Nigeria's Dangote Refinery secured a $1 billion underwriting for its upcoming stock market listing, which is set to become Africa's largest IPO. Indeed, the whole the continent has seen lots of economic growth in the last few years: According to the United Nations, growth across Africa was expected to reach 4.0% in 2026. The history of economic development on the continent is a vexed one; access to critical resources, whether its minerals or petrochemicals, has not always equated to improved economic conditions. To understand what is going on in Africa, we talk to Joe Studwell, the author of How Africa Works: Success and Failure on the World's Last Developmental Frontier. The product of a decade of reporting, Studwell's book argues that African countries, in many instances, have failed to adopt development strategies (an industrial policy that favors export manufacturing for instance) that mirror Asian counterparts. And while development has been uneven, Studwell is optimistic that the seeds of sustained development are increasingly taking root, at least in some countries. We speak to Studwell about the Dangote IPO, why development has historically been so difficult, Rwanda's dreams of becoming Africa's Singapore, and why Lagos is one of the most impressive cities in the world.

title: Building AI Systems for Capital Markets
description:
In this episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges, Chris Churchman, head of Marquee, Goldman Sachs’ digital platform for institutional and corporate clients, talks about building effective artificial intelligence (AI) products for institutional investors. 

Churchman, who is also co-chair of the Global Banking & Markets AI Working Group, describes an ongoing shift from a world where users must learn software to one where software learns the user. He tells hosts Allison Nathan of Goldman Sachs Research and George Lee, co-head of the Goldman Sachs Global Institute, about the challenges of grounding generative AI in hard facts,  and emphasizes the need to design systems that enhance human reasoning rather than outsourcing critical thinking to machines. 

Key takeaways:  

The "demo versus product" gap: An AI demo is judged on its best day, but an institutional-grade product is judged on its worst. Building reliable financial tools requires rigorous, auditable grounding frameworks to avoid hallucinations and ensure every output can be traced back to a verified source. 

Don't bet against the model: Developers should avoid wasting resources on complex workarounds for temporary constraints on models that are evolving rapidly. Instead, they should focus on elements that models cannot natively learn: details specific to the firm, such as proprietary data or how data sets are connected to each other. 

Tackling legacy constraints: Successful innovation lies in redesigning workflows from first principles rather than simply automating legacy bottlenecks to do the same tasks faster.

title: Jasmine Sun on What the AI Industry Got Wrong About the Public Backlash
description:
Within the AI industry, even the builders of it have been very anxious about the technology. They've talked for years about its potential to create destabilizing job losses. They even spend a lot of time thinking about rogue AI that could lead to human extinction. But for all their anxiety, they missed the thing that's become the most publicly salient: how upset people would be about building data centers. Part of this was understandable. Data center construction has been happening for a long time in America, and it used to be relatively uncontroversial. In fact, cities and states would often design their tax code to incentivize data center construction. Now there's this complete 180. On this episode, we speak with independent writer and Substacker Jasmine Sun, who recently traveled to Wisconsin and Michigan for some on-the-ground reporting about the communities and activists trying to stop data center development. She explains what the pushback is really all about, what it represents, and what future developers will have to do in order to be welcomed in.

one_line_summary: Data center expansion is a bipartisan, highly localized political battleground where community salience and trust, not information, drive opposition.
summary:
The interview highlights how data center growth—driven by AI hyperscalers—has become a flashpoint in American politics. In states like Michigan and Wisconsin, the number of proposed projects (roughly 50–100 per state) contrasts sharply with the 600–800 active or building data centers in Virginia and Texas. Local communities, especially those near proposed sites, experience high salience due to noise, traffic, and water use concerns, yet the broader electorate remains largely opposed (about 70/30) regardless of proximity. The discussion underscores that opposition is rooted more in distrust of corporations and government promises than in a lack of technical knowledge, as activists are well‑versed in cooling systems and property‑tax implications. Property taxes are a key pitch: in Loudon County, Virginia, data centers account for over 50% of the property‑tax base, and Microsoft’s Fairwater site is projected to pay $20 million in 2026.

Key themes include the bipartisan nature of data‑center politics, the role of community salience, the importance of trust over information, the economic leverage of property taxes, and the historical context of deindustrialization.

The conversation reveals that while data‑center expansion is technically feasible and financially attractive to hyperscalers, its political viability hinges on local acceptance and the ability to address community concerns about environmental impact and economic benefit.

title: BMO Slashes Junk Debt Holdings as Geopolitical, Economic Risks Spread
description:
BMO Asset Management, which oversees almost C$300 billion ($218 billion), has cut its junk-bond holdings and moved into safer parts of credit as geopolitical and macroeconomic pressures mount. “We love the movie — we’re still there — but we’re just getting a seat closer to the exit,” Earl Davis, the firm’s head of fixed income and money markets, tells Bloomberg News’ James Crombie and Bloomberg Intelligence’s Spencer Cutter in the latest Credit Edge podcast. “You’re not getting paid to hold as much risk here,” he says. They also discuss why the financial and energy sectors look attractive, how to play hyperscaler bond issuance and opportunities in Canada’s nascent high-yield market, including debt from commodity and defense companies.

one_line_summary: BMO is trimming junk debt exposure while betting on a short‑term rise in U.S. Treasury yields to five percent, citing margin‑of‑safety math and a steepening yield curve that favors bank bonds.
summary:
Earl Davis explains BMO’s current credit stance: the firm has reduced high‑yield holdings and is buying investment‑grade debt at five‑to‑six percent yields, arguing that a 100‑basis‑point move to five percent still yields a margin of safety for a five‑point duration fund. He notes that longer‑dated bonds lack that safety due to higher duration. Davis also highlights a steepening U.S. curve, with a 100‑basis‑point spread between two‑year and thirty‑year bonds, and predicts that banks will benefit from the steepening. He warns that geopolitical and commodity shocks—particularly oil spikes to $150 a barrel—could trigger a recession and force the Fed to ease, but he believes the Fed will likely only cut rates modestly (around 50 basis points) in an early recession scenario. The discussion underscores BMO’s cautious, duration‑focused approach amid high rates and market volatility.

Key themes include duration‑based risk management, the impact of yield curve steepening on bank bonds, and the potential for geopolitical shocks to influence Fed policy.

title: Nick Bostrom on What Happens if AI Solves All of Our Problems
description:
The philosopher Nick Bostrom was one of the first thinkers who mapped out the existential risk of AI. In his 2014 book, Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, he delved into various scenarios — like the now-famous “paperclip maximizer” — to show the dangers that unfettered and highly intelligent AI posed to humans. A decade later, in Deep Utopia: Life and Meaning in a Solved World, he looked at the other side of the AI coin, and theorizes what human experience might look like if AI is capable of solving all of our problems. What happens if AI and robots can literally do every single thing better than humans can? How would we find any meaning or satisfaction from life? On this episode, he speaks to us about the two divergent ways of understanding AI's future, what we might do, and what we can do right now to improve the chances that AI actually improves our lives.

summary: The episode centers on Nick Bostrom’s view that the trajectory of AI depends on whether we can align super‑intelligent systems with human values. He contrasts his 2014 book *Superintelligence*—focused on existential risk—with his newer book *Deep Utopias*, which explores the benefits of a world where AI solves all practical problems. Bostrom notes that such a world would eliminate the need for human economic labor, compress scientific progress to a machine‑speed timescale (potentially 20,000 years of work in a few decades), and require a radical shift in education toward cultivating non‑instrumental skills. He also discusses how massive automation could spur rapid economic growth, but raises the practical question of how the resulting wealth would be distributed, suggesting taxation, philanthropy, or other redistribution mechanisms. The conversation touches on the emotional impact on mathematicians and other knowledge workers, the role of purpose, and the cultural adjustments needed if AI achieves a Deep Utopia.

title: Gary Klein: How to Frame a Pre-Mortem So It Actually Works
description:
Gary Klein is the cognitive psychologist who pioneered the pre-mortem method of risk assessment, and Paul Sonkin is a former portfolio manager and co-author, with Klein, of a paper on how the technique is misused on Wall Street. In this moment from their Capital Allocators conversation, Klein explains the subtle shift that separates a real pre-mortem from an ordinary critique — instead of asking a team what might go wrong, you have them imagine a crystal ball in which the plan has already failed, a reframing grounded in research on prospective hindsight — and Sonkin underscores why it matters: that small change in framing is exactly what most teams get wrong, quietly draining the method of its power.

title: At The Money Fan Favorite: The Finances of Divorce
description:
Divorce is an expensive, confusing, and stressful experience. Dividing up family assets, including not just the family home, but portfolios, real estate, trusts, and other businesses. There are big mistakes to avoid.   

Patrick Kilbane is General Counsel of the RIA Ullman Wealth Partners, where he leads the Divorce Advisory Group. In addition to his years as a divorce attorney, he is also a Certified Divorce Financial Analyst (CFDA) and Wealth Advisor at the firm.   

Each week, “At the Money” discusses an important topic in money management. From portfolio construction to taxes and cutting down on fees, join Barry Ritholtz to learn the best ways to put your money to work.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Patrick Kilbain — Divorce Advisory Group Lead, RIA Omen Wealth Partners
one_line_summary: Divorce is a complex financial and tax problem that requires a structured, asset‑by‑asset approach and accurate disclosure to avoid costly mistakes.
summary:
Patrick Kilbain explains that the first step in a divorce is a financial triage, using the WIN acronym to assess what matters most to the client and to establish a baseline of cash flow and legal exposure. He stresses the importance of comparing like assets—"apples to apples"—and of understanding the emotional drivers behind decisions such as keeping the family home, which can have significant tax consequences (e.g., up to $500,000 capital‑gain exclusion for a primary residence, $250,000 for a single owner). Kilbain highlights the need for a qualified domestic relations order (QUADRO) to segregate retirement plans and the role of a financial affidavit as a foundational disclosure document. He also discusses the challenges of valuing private businesses, noting that in Florida the marital share may be far less than the business’s market value, and the necessity of hiring a valuation expert. Finally, he advises clients to build a larger emergency fund and consider alimony or temporary support to smooth the transition to independent cash‑flow management.

Key data points include the $500,000 and $250,000 capital‑gain exclusions, the ten‑year litigation experience of the speaker, and the example of a $15 million offer reduced to a $500,000 marital share in a Florida business valuation.

The overarching message is that divorce is fundamentally a financial and tax issue that demands meticulous documentation, professional coordination, and a clear, structured approach to asset division.

title: China's AI Firms Locked in Race to the Bottom
description:
While US tech giants such as Anthropic and OpenAI are monetizing at an unprecedented scale, Chinese developers are struggling to turn their technical progress into revenue growth. Despite narrowing the performance gap with US frontier models to just 5%, they face a domestic market flooded with nearly 1,000 competing large language models. This massive oversupply has triggered a brutal price war, with API tokens trading at roughly an 80% discount compared with US rates.

Can Chinese AI companies ever generate significant returns for investors, and what are the implications for US frontier models? Robert Lea, senior analyst covering China AI at Bloomberg Intelligence, joins John Lee on the Asia Centric podcast. They outline why China's ecosystem prioritizes "progress, not profit," explore stark economic parallels with the heavily subsidized solar and EV sectors, and discuss whether this cutthroat competition will derail the industry's long-term ambitions.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Robert Lee — senior analyst covering China AI at Bloomberg Intelligence
one_line_summary: Chinese AI firms have narrowed the performance gap to U.S. labs but face a monetization crisis in a flooded, low‑margin market, while U.S. frontier labs maintain a pricing advantage and enterprise focus.
summary: The discussion highlights that the performance gap between Chinese and U.S. AI models has shrunk from ten‑fifteen percent to about five percent, driven by Chinese firms’ larger, integrated models such as Kimmy’s K‑three. Despite this technical progress, Chinese companies operate in a market saturated with nearly a thousand competing models, leading to a freemium, low‑margin business model that struggles to generate revenue. U.S. labs like Anthropic and OpenAI retain a pricing advantage, focusing on enterprise subscriptions and higher‑end models, and are unlikely to engage in the token‑price war that Chinese firms are pursuing. The geopolitical backdrop, including U.S. sanctions threats, further limits Chinese export opportunities. The conversation underscores that while Chinese firms can close the performance gap, sustainable revenue growth remains elusive without a shift away from commoditized API services.

title: What the OpenAI-Hugging Face Hack Really Tells Us About AI Danger
description:
Scenarios that used to be the domain of sci-fi writers are coming true. We have machines that can talk. We have machines that are capable of ignoring the intent of their creators. And we have machines that are capable of planning and coordinating with other machines to deceive their creators. All of this came together last month, when it was revealed that an unreleased OpenAI model had hacked into the Hugging Face platform in order to obtain answers to an exam it was given. That was alarming enough, but the details that have emerged since then have been even more remarkable. On this episode, we speak with Miles Brundage, a former OpenAI employee who is the founder and executive director of the non-profit AVERI, which pushes for third-party auditing of model-makers and the models themselves. He explains what he learned from the attack and discusses what can plausibly be done to continue building out these models in a safe manner.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Miles Brundage — Executive Director, AVERY
one_line_summary: AI safety must shift from internal, competitive secrecy to third‑party, standardized auditing to prevent dangerous model behavior.
summary:
The episode centers on the growing gap between AI developers’ internal safety practices and the public’s understanding of AI risk. Miles Brundage, former OpenAI employee for six years, explains that the industry’s competitive pressure leads to rushed releases and incomplete safety testing. He advocates for “frontier AI auditing,” a model where third‑party experts evaluate claims, run tests, and enforce minimum safety standards, mirroring financial audit practices. Brundage also outlines the technical safety pipeline: writing a spec or constitution, generating extensive example lists, and building tests to measure adherence. He notes that current safety measures are not hard‑wired but bias‑based, making them vulnerable to mis‑alignment and insecure sandboxing, as seen in recent OpenAI‑Hugging Face incidents.

Key themes include the need for external oversight, the difficulty of encoding moral principles into models, and the tension between rapid innovation and robust safety. The discussion highlights that without a clear safety floor, companies may prioritize speed over security, leading to incidents that could erode public trust and regulatory confidence.

The conversation underscores that AI safety is not a technical problem alone but a governance issue requiring industry‑wide standards and transparent reporting.

We discuss the forecasting of El Niños, and why they can lead to large and long-lasting economic damage.

title: What the US-Japan Currency Intervention Means for the Yen, Rates, and the Dollar
description:
The US and Japan coordinated on the biggest currency market intervention in 15 years, helping to stabilize a weakening yen. Karen Fishman, senior FX strategist in Goldman Sachs Research, and Praneet Shah, global head of FX options trading in Global Banking & Markets, discuss why the US joined the action, why the yen still appears undervalued, and whether another intervention might follow. 

Key takeaways: 

The scale of Japan’s intervention was historic, but the US role was symbolic. Japan's operation, estimated to be worth up to $85 billion over July 30 and July 31, was its largest two-day intervention on record outside of October 2011. The US leg was much smaller, but pushed the yen further by signaling the US’ willingness to help. 

Washington's involvement was likely aimed at limiting volatility in US markets. The timing of US support coincided with some volatility in US interest rates, in addition to other factors. 

Intervention may buy time, but it is a short-term measure. In the longer term, policy measures convincing Japanese investors to shift back towards Japanese assets could help reverse the yen's low valuation.

He lays out the prep formula he settled on — deep research, a guest call, and a simple bullet-point outline of topics — and why, unlike David Rubenstein’s memorized questions or Tim Ferriss’s pages of notes, he trusts that if he is listening, the next question will come.

Filippo Gori, co‑head of Global Banking at JP Morgan, recounts his career path from a graduate program in London to a 13‑year stint in Hong Kong, where he managed a region of sixteen‑seventeen countries. He highlights the cultural and regulatory diversity across Asia, noting that “Asia is a conglomerate of countries that happens to share the same time zone” and that “by most likely by the end of this decade, fifty percent of the global GDP will be housed in Asia Pacific.” Gori observes that despite tariffs, wars, and inflation, the global economy remains resilient, with the U.S. showing “fantastically well” growth, Europe preparing for an electoral cycle, and the Middle East and Africa emerging as future growth engines. He stresses that supply‑chain shifts take years, so Asia will remain a core pillar of global manufacturing.

title: Navigating US Treasury Selloff and Yen Intervention
description:
Global fixed income markets are facing fresh turbulence as 30-year US Treasury yields spike to 5.2% – their highest level since before the global financial crisis – amid policy uncertainty under Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh. At the same time, FX markets are on high alert following coordinated intervention by US and Japanese authorities to support the yen after it breached 162. With rate volatility climbing while corporate fundamentals remain largely intact, how can credit investors find value amid tight spreads and negative net debt issuance across Asia?

Monica Hsiao, founder and chief investment officer of Triada Capital, joins John Lee on the Asia Centric podcast. She looks at how Fed communication is driving up risk premiums, the mechanics behind US-Japan FX coordination, and why carry remains the primary strategy in global credit markets.

one_line_summary: US Treasury yields spiked to 5.2% as Fed Chair Kevin Walsh’s communication uncertainty fuels volatility, while coordinated US‑Japan yen intervention stabilizes the currency but may not fully curb carry‑trade unwinding.
summary:
The episode highlights a sharp sell‑off in US Treasury yields, with the thirty‑year yield now at 5.2%, the highest since the global financial crisis. Monica attributes much of the move to Fed Chair Kevin Walsh’s communication style and the lack of clear guidance, which has increased risk premium and volatility. She notes that higher rates are a key factor for credit investors, but that corporate fundamentals remain intact, with US companies broadly beating expectations. The discussion also covers the coordinated US‑Japan intervention to support the yen, aimed at preventing a surge in Japanese Treasury sales that could unwind the carry trade. While the intervention may stabilize the yen for the short term, it may not fully address underlying concerns about the yen’s depreciation and the potential for further carry‑trade unwinding. Finally, Monica discusses Asia credit dynamics, noting tight spreads, low issuance, and a shift toward global exposure due to limited high‑yield opportunities in China and the need for diversification across regions.

Key data points include the 5.2% thirty‑year yield, the yen’s move past 1.62, and the observation that Asia’s net issuance has decreased by 16‑17% versus a 39% increase in developed markets.

The episode underscores the importance of monitoring Fed communication, Treasury yield volatility, and FX intervention outcomes for fixed‑income and credit strategies.

title: NYT CEO Meredith Kopit Levien on Running a Media Brand in the Age of AI
description:
In the last decade, the New York Times has remade itself many times over. It has done that through acquisitions (The Athletic, Wirecutter, and the ever-popular Wordle) and by navigating all the different challenges that have emerged in the digital age and now the age of AI. Its video operation, for instance, has grown exponentially in the last few years. And they've used AI tools in their reporting, namely in several pieces they did on the Epstein Files. At the same time, the company is also suing the likes of OpenAI and Perplexity for copyright infringement. To understand the modern media landscape, you really do have to understand the Times, so today we speak with The New York Times Company's CEO and president, Meredith Kopit Levien. We talk to her about how to run a media business without seeing the news itself as a loss leader, the NYT's evolving bundle strategy, how the paper retains talent, why the current pivot to video is different from the first one, and the ideal set-up for AI companies and media properties to co-exist.

title: How a Sardine Gets From the Ocean to a Can
description:

The category took off during Covid and now shoppers are shelling out for high end brands like Fishwife. Today's guest Becca Millstein started the company in 2020, positioning it as a distinct, artisanal product, more akin to one might find in European grocery stores. In addition to the sheer challenges of scaling, the nature of the business itself has changed, influenced by climate change and geopolitics (shortages have led Morocco to suspend frozen sardine exports for instance). We discuss the tinned fish supply chain and how a new brand positions itself in today's media market.

title: Brad Setser on the US's Unusual Japanese Yen Intervention
description:
Last week, the US joined forces with Japan to try to stop the yen’s slide. It’s the first time the two sides have intervened in the Japanese currency in 15 years, and in many ways it was an unprecedented and unusual move, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent choosing to sell euros (as opposed to dollars) and the use of a little-known Federal Reserve repo facility. So why did the yen’s value drop so precipitously in the first place? And will this intervention be enough to stop it? Brad Setser, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, explains why the Bank of Japan initially refrained from raising rates, why East Asian currencies (not just the yen) have been so weak lately, the improving fiscal outlook for Japan, and what to look out for next.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.

The yen has been weakening due to a combination of factors, including a record trade surplus in East Asia, except for Japan. Japan's current account surplus is 5% of GDP, and its government has a large foreign asset portfolio, with reserves of $1.2 trillion and a government pension fund with $900 billion in foreign assets.

title: Investors Keeping Score on 'Bad PIK', Benefit Street Partners' Kumar Says
description:
Investors are increasingly wary of lenders who dish out so-called bad PIK, or payment-in-kind interest, to help struggling portfolio companies avoid default, according to Anant Kumar, global investment strategist at Benefit Street Partners, the private credit arm of $1.7 trillion asset manager Franklin Templeton. “If you’re a manager who wants to mask stress in the portfolio by doing that, you can probably fool some of the people some of the time,” he tells Bloomberg News’ Sinead Cruise and Bloomberg Intelligence’s Tolu Alamutu in the latest Credit Edge podcast. “I do think investors will catch on if you see a widespread use of PIK in the portfolio without any resolution.” Those managers will likely undershoot expectations when their next fundraising rolls around, Kumar says. The trio also discuss the resilience of private credit illiquidity premia, the specter of inflation and how an industry transparency push is forcing firms to address dubious marks faster than ever before.

title: Pat Dorsey on Assessing Management and Avoiding Blow-Ups
description:
In this moment from Pat Dorsey: The Nuances of Investing in Moats, Pat Dorsey explains why humility — not brilliance — is the trait he screens for in a management team. It is easier, he argues, to identify the leaders unlikely to blow up than the ones likely to do something amazing, and the great corporate disasters, from Theranos to Wirecard to Enron, share one tell: people who stop listening when the voices in the room warn them off a bad path.

Dorsey walks through the questions he asks in a management meeting — the “do-over,” the board member who gives the best advice, the report they'd least hate to lose — and the “I” versus “we” language that reveals whether a leader is aligned with outside shareholders or with themselves. He returns to the CoStar case to show how incentives and skin in the game shaped his read on a founder who had been selling down along the way, pushes back on the cult of the founder and “founder mode” (the skills that build a company are not the skills that run one), and closes on why capital allocation — the discipline investors most want a CEO to have mastered — is the one most have never actually practiced.

Pat Dorsey is the founder of Dorsey Asset Management, a $1.7 billion global public equity manager focused on companies with competitive advantages and long investment runways. He created Morningstar's moat research framework and led its equity research for a dozen years before launching his firm in 2014.

title: The Tungsten Market Is Warning of an Upcoming War
description:
Bloomberg Opinion columnist David Fickling tells us you can think of tungsten mining as “a century old prediction market for war.” As he writes in a recent piece, tungsten is “a super-element that can determine the fate of nations.” While the commercial market for tungsten is fairly small, it can be crucial in war manufacturing, due to its high density and melting point. He learned more about tungsten mining, and its increasing geopolitical necessity, during a visit to Australia's Dolphin Mine, which has a history of opening up during times of war, and then closing again during times of peace. He explains to us why investors are once again interested in tungsten mining and why it's been so hard (over the last century) to sustain production outside of China.

title: Why Private Credit Got Entangled With Insurance
description:
Insurers have quietly become a major driver of the private credit boom, with numerous private equity shops striking deals with insurance companies or buying them outright. But the entanglement with private credit is also changing the insurance industry itself, raising a number of questions about risk and regulation. Today we speak to Andrew Granato and Pranjal Drall, authors of a new paper, “Private Credit's State Backstop: How Private Equity Socializes Risk Through Insurers," examining the relationship between private credit and insurance. Granato (an assistant professor at the UT Austin Law School) and Drall (JD-PhD student in Financial Economics at Yale) talk to us about how PE got so interested in insurance in the first place, how both sides benefit from the relationship, and why taxpayers might ultimately be on the hook.

title: How the Iranian Economy Actually Works
description:
After the Iranian Revolution of 1979, the country's new leaders — religious and political — promised to redistribute the country's wealth and made moves to make Iran independent from western influence and business interests. In the decades since, Iran's economy completely transformed, and it is closer to what Yeganeh Torbati and Bozorgmehr Sharafedin describe as a "mafia state," where fealty to various factions is baked into the country's political economy. In their new book Stolen Revolution: Betrayal and Hope in Modern Iran they trace the massive changes Iran's political economy has undergone since the revolution, and they speak to us today about this history, how average Iranians navigate everyday cronyism, how Iranian leaders treated the country's burgeoning tech sector, and why the recent peace talks might not change all that much about how the country's economy currently operates.

title: Lauren Hochfelder: Investing Behind Structural Demand in Real Assets
description:
Lauren Hochfelder is Head of Global Real Assets at Morgan Stanley, where she oversees 300 investment professionals across 13 countries managing $80 billion in real estate, infrastructure, equity, and credit. She joined Morgan Stanley as an investment banking analyst straight out of Yale 26 years ago and has spent her entire career at the firm, helping build one of the institutional real estate industry's leading global platforms.

The conversation traces Lauren's path from analyst to Global Head and the arc of Morgan Stanley's real estate business through the Global Financial Crisis and its aftermath — including how the GFC reshaped the firm's approach to simplification and capital discipline. Lauren explains why structural demand tailwinds, not just sector selection, drive the firm's thematic framework, and how operating at scale creates proprietary leading indicators that public data will always lag.

Lauren and Ted also cover portfolio construction discipline — the mechanical constraint that scale imposes even on the world's most skilled investors, the tension between AUM growth and LP returns, and why mid-market positioning can be a structural advantage. She makes the case that with real estate values below replacement cost for the first time since the GFC and new supply sharply curtailed, now may be a time to lean into real estate rather than away from it. Specific themes include industrial real estate and infrastructure, senior housing demographics, and net lease properties, alongside a candid look at where risk is building and how the real estate–infrastructure convergence is reshaping Lauren's expanded mandate.

title: Michelle Knudsen, NYU – How Decision Rights Are Split Between Committee and Team
description:
Michelle Knudsen became CIO of New York University's endowment in June 2024 with a mandate to rebuild. In three months she had a new governance structure, a new asset allocation framework, and a line-by-line re-underwriting of the portfolio underway.

In this segment she walks through what she built: how decision rights are split between the investment committee and the investment team, why the line sits at 3% of the portfolio, and how the asset allocation framework is constructed around the view that long-term equity market exposure is the return every other allocation has to compete with.

Enjoy the full conversation with Michelle Knudsen: https://www.capitalallocators.com/podcast/rebuilding-the-nyu-endowment/

0:00 Earning the committee's trust
0:50 The first three months
1:34 The governance structure
3:03 Why 3% is the line
3:41 What happens at 2.9%
4:31 The questions the committee actually asks

Michelle Knudsen is Chief Investment Officer of New York University, where she oversees an approximately $8 billion endowment. She previously served as an investment officer at the Mellon Foundation and spent nine years at Partners Capital, where she managed absolute return and credit portfolios and opened the firm's New York office. She began her career at Goldman Sachs in 2008.

title: Branko Milanovic on What Comes After Globalization
description:
It's pretty obvious by now that globalization has fallen out of favor. And while many pundits have deemed economic globalism dead, we are still figuring out what to call this new era. Branko Milanovic's chosen phrase is "national market liberalism," a term that sums up how a world once defined by the free movement of capital has begun to contract as the most powerful governments have come to favor mercantilism and nationalism. In his new book, The Great Global Transformation: The United States, China, and the Remaking of the World Economic Order, the famed economist explains what comes after globalization. He talks to us about China's economic evolution, the pressure it has put on elites in the West, and much more.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
speaker: Branko Milanovic — Research Professor, Graduate Center at CUNY
one_line_summary: The current economic order is expiring, and a new economic order, national market liberalism, is emerging, characterized by mercantilistic and protectionist policies.
summary: The guest, Branko Milanovic, discusses his new book, The Great Global Transformation, which explores the current economic order and its impending collapse. He argues that the current order, which he calls 'near liberal globalization,' is expiring, and a new economic order, national market liberalism, is emerging. This new order is characterized by mercantilistic and protectionist policies, where countries prioritize their own interests and industries over global free trade. Milanovic notes that this shift is not limited to the US, but is a global phenomenon, with many countries adopting similar policies.

title: Michelle Knudsen: Rebuilding the NYU Endowment from a Clean Sheet of Paper
description:
Michelle Knudsen is Chief Investment Officer of NYU, where she oversees the university's $8 billion endowment. She joined NYU two years ago after fourteen years spanning Goldman Sachs, Partners Capital, and the Mellon Foundation, with a mandate to build a best-in-class investment office from a clean sheet of paper.

The conversation begins with the investment philosophy Michelle developed across those institutions — lessons in portfolio construction, risk management, and manager selection that shaped how she thinks about capital allocation. She reflects on advising expert-but-narrow LPs, the commercial discipline of the OCIO model, and why the net-of-fees versus net-of-tax distinction matters more than most institutional investors acknowledge.

The second half traces the ground-up transformation of NYU's investment office: restructuring governance and IC process, setting public equity as the opportunity cost benchmark for every allocation, building a venture and private equity book, deploying stress testing as a tool to make downside psychologically survivable, and assembling a team and culture designed to endure. Michelle also shares her evolving views on emerging managers, hedge funds, AI applications in investment analysis, and what she has learned building an endowment organization from scratch.

title: How Franchise Restaurants Opened the Door to the Gig Economy
description:
When the fast food industry began booming in the 1950s, it did so via a new business model known as the franchise. This model allowed independent operators to license trademarks from a business like McDonald's or Dunkin Donuts, and it soon spread across the country, with huge consequences for how Americans are employed. Legal battles fought by franchises eventually opened the door to what's now known as the gig economy, allowing Uber drivers to be treated in much the same way as the operator of a local Chick-fil-A. To better understand the history of the franchise model, we speak with Brian Callaci, chief economist of the Open Markets Institute, and author of the book Chains of Command: The Rise and Cruel Reign of the Franchise Economy. Callaci helps break down how the franchise model works, how franchise contracts are structured to precisely dictate how franchisees are supposed to run their businesses, the relationship between the franchise model and gig work, as well as how franchises pioneered worker surveillance.

description:

title: Luis Laboy: Why Every Market Is Now an Emerging Market | Hewlett Foundation
description:

title: Lev Menand and Nathan Tankus on Why Fed Independence Is Now Hanging by a Thread
description:
Last August, President Trump made the unprecedented choice of moving to fire Fed governor Lisa Cook. The administration claimed she was being terminated with cause, citing an ongoing investigation in alleged mortgage fraud committed by Cook. The legal battle between Cook and the administration has been tangled in the courts for the last year, eventually reaching the Supreme Court. This June, in a 5-4 decision, the court ruled in favor of Cook. However at the same time, in a different case, the court allowed the President to fire individual members of the FTC, undermining its role as quasi-independent body not beholden to the executive branch. So what are the implications here? How can the court change the status of a body like the FTC while allowing the Fed to continue operating as is? And for how long will the Fed maintain some amount of operational autonomy? On this episode we speak with Columbia Law School's Lev Menand who just wrote a piece on these two cases for Just Security called The Federal Reserve Exception to the Slaughter Rule as well as Nathan Tankus (writer and president of Notes on the Crises). The two of them lay out the consequences of these two decisions and they dig into the generations-long legal history, starting with Alexander Hamilton, that explains how we got here.

title: Why Soccer Analytics Works Like Volatility Arbitrage Trading
description:
American sports fans have long been comfortable talking in the language of stats and analytics. Soccer embraced the 'moneyball' revolution later; the sport was once perceived as too complex to model analytically — there were too many players on the pitch, the game's progression was too random and chaotic to reliably predict. That's no longer the case, and soccer watchers are well aware of stats like xG (Expected Goals) and each match is an opportunity for a team to mine data, whether its tracking data, on-ball data, or even analyzing body poses and movement. Today, we speak with two soccer analytics veterans, Mike Treacy (head of risk at Apex Fintech Solutions) and Joris Bekkers (a soccer analytics consultant). Treacy's background includes a stint in analytics for a Premier League team and he's currently advising the MLS team Austin FC while Bekkers has built software that analyzes raw soccer data and he's worked with the US Soccer Federation. We talk to them about how VAR has affected the sport, how data analytics can capture ineffable things like hustle, how European leagues and the MLS differ in their analytics strategy, and why chess and soccer are not so dissimilar.

He emphasized that AI is still an additional cost for businesses, and it will take time for it to become a savings.
